sentences.text: Adult Europasaurus was a very small sauropod, reaching lengths of 5.7 to 6.2 meters and weighing between 750 and 2,100 kilograms.
Younger individuals of Europasaurus ranged in size from 1.75 meters for the youngest juveniles up to 3.7 meters.
One distinguishing feature of Europasaurus is that its ankle bone, the astragalus, is twice as wide as it is tall.
Most external skull bones of Europasaurus are preserved, with the exception of the prefrontals.
Eight premaxillae of Europasaurus show a rectangular snout shape similar to that of Camarasaurus.
The two processes of the quadratojugal bone in Europasaurus diverge at nearly 90 degrees, with the dorsal process curving to match the quadrate.
Adult Europasaurus neck vertebrae have an elongated shape with a ball-shaped front end and a notch on the top of the rear end.
Fossilized skin impressions of Europasaurus relatives show scales but lack bony plates or nodules that would indicate armor.
Europasaurus possesses unique "twisted" teeth that serve as a potential diagnostic feature for identifying isolated teeth belonging to the Brachiosauridae family.
It is suggested that Europasaurus's ancestor shrank in size after migrating to an island in northern Germany smaller than 200,000 square kilometers that could not support large sauropods.
Europasaurus represents the only significant case of rapid body mass reduction in derived Sauropodomorpha, contrasting with the general trend of size increase in the group.
The first fossil of Europasaurus, a single tooth, was found in 1998 by private collector Holger Lüdtke at the Langenberg Mountain quarry in Germany.
The species was formally described and named Europasaurus holgeri in 2006.
The species name 'holgeri' was chosen to honor Holger Lüdtke, who discovered the initial fossils.
A partial sauropod skull, the first of its kind found in Europe, was revealed in January 2002.
By 2014, approximately 1,300 vertebrate bones had been prepared from the fossil-bearing layer, most of which belonged to Europasaurus.
The genus Europasaurus was named by Sander et al. in 2006.
Europasaurus developed its small size due to a significantly reduced growth rate compared to larger sauropods like Camarasaurus.
Researchers proposed that Europasaurus's small size was caused by pedomorphism, where adults retained juvenile characteristics.
Infant Europasaurus were likely precocial but relied on adult herd protection, a behavior not seen in larger sauropods due to size differences.
The long inner ear structure suggests Europasaurus had keen hearing and engaged in gregarious behavior for intraspecific communication.
Over 450 bones of Europasaurus were found at Langenberg Quarry, with about one-third showing tooth marks from predators.
The abundance of Europasaurus fossils suggests a herd drowned while crossing a tidal zone.
Europasaurus is classified as a basal macronarian sauropod, a type of quadrupedal herbivorous dinosaur.
The genus name Europasaurus means 'Europe lizard'.
Upon its initial description, Europasaurus was classified within Macronaria but outside the families Brachiosauridae and the clade Titanosauromorpha.
Later phylogenetic analyses placed Europasaurus as a basal camarasauromorph that is more closely related to titanosaurs than to Camarasaurus.
Europasaurus belongs to the parent group Camarasauromorpha.
Europasaurus lived in northern Germany during the Late Jurassic, specifically between 154 and 151 million years ago.
Europasaurus lived in an island ecosystem in northern Germany during the late Jurassic, from the early Oxfordian to late Kimmeridgian.
Europasaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian stage, between 152.21 and 149.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether Europasaurus is a true brachiosaurid, as some analyses place it there despite the lack of key diagnostic bones like caudal vertebrae.
Some phylogenetic studies identify Europasaurus as the most basal member of the Brachiosauridae family.
Researchers suggest that larger theropods arriving on the island likely caused the extinction of Europasaurus and other dwarf fauna.
